$comment: R1761 — THE DASHBOARD SECTION'S PAINTED SURFACES, written down from the
behaviour reference in neutral vocabulary, so the section can be judged
against something other than its own tables.
WHY THIS IS A SECOND DOCUMENT FOR ONE SCREEN, WHICH IS NORMALLY A DEFECT.
`analyzer-board-spec.json` beside it already specifies five surfaces of
this same screen. They are not the same kind of claim, and the difference
is the one R1758 made the report carry: a surface here is read back out of
a PAINTED FRAME, at any moment, by a running application answering a host.
Two of that file's five are not paint at all — a drop contract is a
declaration a surface publishes, and a drop standing is what a router hands
a source mid-gesture — and the other three exist only while a placement is
in flight, which a wire read cannot arrange.
So that document is judged by a DRIVEN sweep, which can perform a gesture
and ask the declaration; this one is judged from the frame. Splitting them
by evidence rather than by screen is what keeps a section's published
verdict honest: a paint-stamped report that quietly answered two of its
surfaces from a declaration would be exactly the defect R1758 repaired one
level up. The two documents name DISJOINT surfaces and a gate asserts it,
because one word with two documents behind it is the defect R1747 spent a
round on.
WHAT IS THE REFERENCE'S AND WHAT IS THIS BUILD'S. The layout bar's four
parts, the panel's heading and hint, the three groups, the entries' order
inside the first two groups, the footer's two counts and the four cards the
board opens with are all the reference's, read off the screen it states.
Two things are not, and both are recorded as remainders below rather than
written in as if they were: this build's hint offers a second way to place
a widget, and its third group is named for a wider set than the reference's
third.
★ THE ENTRY LIST IS THE REFERENCE'S OWN COUNT, NOT ITS OWN LIST. The
reference's palette PAINTS six reserved entries and its footer says NINE
are reserved — the mismatch is in the reference, and the requirement table
on the same page names all nine. This build lists nine, so its panel and
its footer agree; the three the reference's panel omits sit in the group
their requirement belongs to. Stated here rather than left for a reader to
notice, because a pin that silently completed its source would be a pin
nobody could check against the source.
HOW A PART IS TITLED, AND WHY IT DIFFERS PER SURFACE. Where the reference
fixes the WORDS a reader reads — a panel's heading, a group's heading —
the title here is those words, and the judge reads them back out of the
frame. Where a part is a value or a control whose label the screen changes
as it works, the title is this screen's own name for it and what the pin
fixes is the roster and its order. `crate::judge` says which is which per
surface and why.

owed.sentence: `hint` is specified as "Drag onto the canvas to place" and reads "Drag onto the canvas, or click to add"
owed.why: The reference offers one way to get a widget onto the board and this build offers two: every placeable row carries a seat that places one without a drag, which the reference draws as well and does not mention here. The line says both, so a reader is not told to drag when a click will do. Recorded rather than reconciled by deleting the second way, which is the direction this project's rule about the reference runs: what the reference has and this build lacks is built, and what this build has beyond it is kept.

owed.sentence: `operate` is specified as "DIAGNOSTICS · RELEASE 2" and reads "DIAGNOSE & OPERATE · RELEASE 2"
owed.why: The reference's third group holds three diagnostic widgets. This build's third group holds those and two that ACT on the system under study rather than report on it, so a heading saying only diagnostics would misname half of what is under it. The group's membership is the reference's requirement table's; the heading follows the membership.
